title: Hoctor v. United States Department of Agriculture
lead: An exotic-animal dealer built a six-foot perimeter fence after a federal veterinarian suggested it. Years later, inspectors cited him under an internal memorandum demanding eight feet, raising the question whether the agency had interpreted an existing regulation or created a new rule.

actors.name: Hoctor
actors.role: Licensed exotic-animal dealer operating near Terre Haute, Indiana.

actors.name: United States Department of Agriculture (USDA)
actors.role: Agency that regulated animal housing and sanctioned Hoctor.

actors.name: Chief Judge Posner
actors.role: Author of the Seventh Circuit panel opinion, joined by Judges Diane P. Wood and Evans.

proceedings: Hoctor sought review only of the sanction tied to the eight-foot perimeter-fence memorandum. The Seventh Circuit vacated the Department’s order insofar as it rested on that requirement because the agency had not used required notice-and-comment rulemaking.
limits: The decision reserved USDA’s ultimate statutory authority to require the fence and possible enforcement based on a case-specific finding of unsafe containment. Other violations were outside the challenge. This account concerns the 1996 ruling, not current fencing or regulatory-deference rules.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A dealer installs several layers of animal containment
sections.cue: What did the initial inspector recommend?
paragraphs: The Animal Welfare Act authorized the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) to establish standards for humane animal handling, housing, and related treatment, and to sanction licensed dealers for violations. Using notice and comment, USDA adopted a structural-strength regulation requiring appropriately constructed, structurally sound, and maintained housing facilities that protected and contained the animals. Nobody disputed that regulation’s validity.

Hoctor began dealing in exotic animals near Terre Haute in 1982. His twenty-five-acre compound contained individual animal pens, a containment fence around the area of the pens, and a perimeter fence around the entire compound. His animals included lions, tigers, ligers, cougars, and snow leopards. A USDA veterinarian inspecting the operation at the outset suggested a six-foot perimeter fence, which Hoctor built. That outer fence was a backup to two other layers, not the animals’ ordinary enclosure.

sections.title: An internal memorandum introduces a fixed height
sections.cue: How did a six-foot fence become the basis for a sanction?
paragraphs: In 1983, USDA circulated an internal memorandum instructing inspectors that dangerous animals had to be inside a perimeter fence at least eight feet high. The agency called the instruction an interpretation of its structural-strength regulation. Inspectors began citing Hoctor for his six-foot fence in 1990, and USDA eventually sanctioned him for that and other alleged violations.

Replacing the fence would cost this small dealer many thousands of dollars. At appellate argument, counsel reported that Hoctor had stopped dealing in big cats while the dispute continued. Hoctor limited his judicial challenge to the fence requirement, and both parties agreed that this part of the sanction depended on the memorandum’s validity as an interpretive rule.

There had been a serious containment incident: two lions escaped a pen, and Hoctor shot them because they came dangerously close to an employee. The lions remained inside the separate containment fence. The appellate court recognized possible reasons for fail-safe protection, including protection of the animals, but did not treat that episode as establishing the need for an eight-foot outer fence. USDA defended this sanction solely under its memorandum, not a case-specific finding that the actual arrangement was unsafe.

sections.title: USDA invokes interpretation rather than legislative rulemaking
paragraphs: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) generally required notice and comment for legislative rules while exempting interpretative rules and general policy statements. Chief Judge Posner, writing for a panel with Judges Diane P. Wood and Evans, recognized the exemption’s practical purpose. Agencies must interpret uncertain law during enforcement; lengthy rulemaking for every new interpretive question could obstruct enforcement and discourage useful advance guidance.

But selecting a new binding standard under delegated legislative authority required participation and a statement of basis and purpose. Calling a standard an interpretation did not settle which category applied.

USDA invoked deference to its interpretation of its own regulation. It argued that secure containment included height and that a six-foot fence lacked structural strength in the missing two feet. The panel doubted that language about sound construction and repair naturally concerned an animal’s ability to jump over a fence. More fundamentally, consistency with the regulation was insufficient: the new requirement had to be derivable through a process reasonably described as interpretation.

sections.title: Eight feet reflects a policy selection rather than a discovered meaning
sections.cue: Why did this requirement need public participation?
paragraphs: The general goal of secure containment did not contain a latent eight-foot dimension. Seven-and-a-half, nine, or ten feet might also serve it. The memorandum’s additional requirement of three feet between perimeter fences and animal pens presented the same unexplained numerical selection. Describing that choice as arbitrary meant choosing among alternatives, not necessarily that the result was arbitrary or capricious on its merits.

Nor could USDA avoid procedures by relying directly on the statute’s authorization to establish minimum standards. Where Congress delegated the creation of duties rather than prescribing them, an agency’s new binding standard was legislative. Assuming authority to require eight feet therefore established possible power to legislate, not an exemption from the method of legislating.

Notice and comment mattered because different reasonable choices imposed different burdens. Many dealers might face costly replacements. Their concerns deserved systematic consideration before USDA selected a binding dimension and explained it. The prospect of numerous comments strengthened the case for participation; it did not excuse skipping the process.

sections.title: The panel identifies interpretations that might legitimately use numbers
sections.cue: What made this memorandum different from a scientific measure or rebuttable presumption?
paragraphs: The court did not hold that every numerical rule was legislative. Established scientific criteria could translate a general norm into a number by interpretation. A rebuttable rule of thumb might also remain connected to the underlying standard. USDA would have been on stronger ground had it presumed lower fences unsafe while allowing a dealer to demonstrate adequate containment.
This memorandum instead imposed a flat, self-contained requirement. Counsel’s appellate suggestions that a moat or electrified six-foot fence might suffice could not amend the agency’s actual rule.

The panel declined to rely on USDA’s use of notice and comment for fencing requirements involving other animals. Agencies could voluntarily use those procedures even when unnecessary, and should not be penalized for partial procedural compliance. Agency intent and labels likewise supplied weak evidence; classification depended on the pronouncement’s nature.

sections.title: The sanction loses its procedural foundation
sections.cue: What did vacatur decide—and leave open?
paragraphs: The Seventh Circuit vacated the Department’s order insofar as it rested on the eight-foot perimeter-fence requirement. That binding numerical standard could not be derived through interpretation and had not been adopted through the required process. There was no separate opinion.

The court did not decide that USDA lacked statutory authority ever to require such a fence. It also reserved whether actual unsafe containment could support enforcement on a different, case-specific theory. Other violations were outside Hoctor’s limited judicial challenge. The decision resolved the procedure needed for this particular inflexible standard, not every animal-safety question at the compound.
